food.text: Peruvian cuisine grew from four traditional staples: corn, potatoes and other tubers, Amaranthaceae such as quinoa, and legumes. After the Spaniards arrived in the 1530s, they brought rice, wheat and meats such as beef, pork and chicken to the mix.

Before citrus fruits reached the Andean region in the 16th century, ancient Andean coastal inhabitants marinated fish in juices from native plants. One example was the banana passionfruit, known locally as tumbo. Lemon and lime came later.

Inca cuisine, which lasted into the 16th century, relied on tubers, roots and grains as its most important plant staples. Common meats came from guinea pigs, llamas and fish. Terraces built at different altitudes in the mountains let the Incas cultivate a wide number of staples.

The modern style of ceviche resulted from a culinary fusion during the Spanish colonial era in the 16th century. Historians agree that it originated in present-day Peru, through the introduction of limes, onions and vinegar.

Roots and tubers provided the staples of the Inca, but they were still ranked lower than maize. Achira, a sweet, starchy root baked in earth ovens, had to be transported up to the power center of Cuzco.

In 1527 the Spanish started to bring people from Africa, and Spanish slaving from Africa contributed to Peru's diversity. Lima's population was 30 to 40 percent of African descent, and the women did domestic work or vended food. African influence played a role in shaping Peru's national food heritage.

The technique of macerating raw fish and meat in vinegar, citrus and spices, called escabeche, was brought to the Americas from Spain. It is linked to the Moorish heritage in Spanish cuisine, and it helped shape ceviche.

Peru, as a Spanish colony, has a history of involvement in the slave trade, with enslaved people imported from Ghana, Angola, Nigeria, the Republic of Congo, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mozambique and Madagascar. They were typically imported to perform labor in sugar cane, cotton fields and vineyards, with very few in gold mines in Cuzco. Their African descendants brought their own dances and drumming music, along with some culinary art characterized by its delicious taste.

Salt loaves found in the Sierras del Opón were of much higher quality than Caribbean coast salt. Natives said they came from an advanced and rich civilisation high up in the Andes to the south, which drew the Spanish into the mountains on a journey called the Camino de la Sal. By early March 1537, almost a year after more than 700 soldiers left Santa Marta, diseases, hunger, native attacks and jaguars had heavily reduced the army.

The chef Gastón Acurio explains that Lima was the capital of the Viceroyalty of Peru, which at one point included most of western South America. That position let popular dishes such as ceviche travel to other provinces and become local cuisine with regional flavors.

Like other American peoples, the Inca ate animals that many Europeans considered vermin, such as frogs, caterpillars, beetles and ants. Mayfly larvae were eaten raw, or toasted and ground to make loaves that could then be stored.

art.text: The Cusco school began after the 1534 Spanish conquest of Peru. It is considered the first artistic center in the Americas to systematically teach European artistic techniques. It was based in Cusco, the former capital of the Inca Empire.

An Ángel arcabucero is an angel carrying an arquebus, an early firearm, instead of the traditional sword. These angels wear clothing inspired by that of Criollo and Andean nobles. The style arose in Peru in the second half of the 17th century and was especially common in the Cusco School.

The Crown of the Andes was made for a statue of the Virgin Mary in the cathedral of Popayán, Colombia. It is adorned with 450 emeralds. Its oldest parts, the orb and cross, date to the 16th century, the diadem to around 1660, and the arches to around 1770.

The Italian Jesuit painter Bernardo Bitti arrived in Cusco in 1583, and his arrival marks the start of Cuzqueño art's development. He introduced Mannerism, a fashionable European current that treated figures in a somewhat elongated way, with the light focused on them.

Marcos Zapata was the most important artist of the 18th century in the Cusco school. His output of more than 200 paintings spans 1748 to 1764. His best works are fifty large canvases covering the high arches of the Cathedral of Cusco, rich in flora and fauna as decoration.

Under Spanish rule, Bolivia's original architecture blended with European Baroque to form a style called Andean Baroque, found in most of its cities. Potosí, the largest silver supplier for Spain, is the most representative example. About 160,000 Spanish colonists lived there in the 17th century.

Luis de Riaño was born in Lima and studied under the Italian artist Angelino Medoro. Bolivian historians say he dominated the local art scene between 1618 and 1640. Among his works are the murals of the church of Andahuaylillas.

In 1688, after continuous conflicts, the corporation of painters in Cusco split, and the Amerindian-Quechua and Mestizo painters were removed from it. They said they had been exploited by their Spanish colleagues. Free of the corporation's impositions, these artists followed their own sensibility and put their way of seeing the world onto the canvas.

The Church of Calamarca, about 60 km from La Paz, Bolivia, holds the most complete surviving series of ángeles arcabuceros. Notable examples include the Asiel Timor Dei by the Master of Calamarca, painted around 1680.

The largest emerald on the Crown of the Andes is called the Atahualpa Emerald. It might have belonged to the Incan Emperor Atahualpa and been seized from him when Francisco Pizarro captured him in 1532.

In the late 18th century, native weavers adapted their techniques for a colonial audience. Bedcovers, table covers, rugs and wall hangings became popular formats. European influences brought lace-inspired borders and stylized circular patterns into Andean textiles.

According to Kelly Donahue-Wallace, the arquebusier angel genre probably began in the Collao region near Lake Titicaca and was based on Spanish and Dutch engravings. Another likely source for the angels' poses was the 1607 Exercise in Arms by Jacob de Gheyn II, which showed military drills of the period.

war.text: On November 16, 1532, the tiny army of Francisco Pizarro began the Spanish conquest of Peru, taking advantage of the Inca Civil War. In the following decades Spain consolidated its power over the entire Andean region, repressing successive indigenous rebellions.

The rebellion of Túpac Amaru II, which lasted from 1780 to 1783, was the largest revolt in the colonial Americas and the most devastating to the Viceroyalty of Peru. It began in the Cusco region and spread to modern-day Bolivia and Argentina.

In early March 1537, almost a year after the original group of more than 700 soldiers left Santa Marta, the army reached Muisca territory in Chipatá, heavily reduced by diseases, hunger, native attacks and jaguars. The expedition of Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada had been the hardest of the main conquests of the Americas. The indigenous people gave the surviving Spanish cotton mantles against the cold of the Altiplano.

Declining silver production diminished royal income, so the Crown enacted the Bourbon Reforms, which increased taxes and partitioned the Viceroyalty. These new laws provoked Túpac Amaru II's rebellion and other revolts, all of which were suppressed.

After Viceroy Francisco de Toledo organized the viceroyalty in 1572, he promptly declared war on Vilcabamba, the last refuge of the Inca. Soon afterwards Tupac Amaru, the last Inca emperor, was captured and executed in Cuzco.
In 1742 Juan Santos Atahualpa led a rebellion in the Andean jungle provinces of Tarma and Jauja. It expelled the Spanish from a large area.

On August 19 and 20, 1538, Spanish conquistadors under Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada fought the Panche at Tocarema, allied with the Muisca zipa Sagipa. The Panche fired poisoned arrows from the hills; the Muisca guecha warriors lost around one hundred dead and many more wounded, and 30 Spanish were wounded, none fatally. The Spanish and Muisca won.

In April 1537 the Spanish defeated the zipa Tisquesusa and his guecha warriors. Strange light-skinned men had told him that he would "die, bathing in his own blood", and the Spanish dealt him a lethal wound.

At Tocarema the Panche had used the hills and poisoned arrows against the Muisca, then retreated at night. The next morning they attacked the Muisca in open terrain, and the Spanish conquistadors came out of hiding with their cavalry and weapons. Juan de Sanct Martín commanded the right flank and Juan de Céspedes the left.

Spanish rule did not fully end Panche resistance in western Cundinamarca after Tocarema, and later expeditions were needed to subdue them. Early chroniclers such as Pedro Simón described these neighbours of the Muisca as bellicose and cannibalistic, and Pedro de Aguado also called them cannibals. Afterwards the Spanish set up three encomiendas in Panche territory: Honda, Calamoyma and Chapayma.

In the Battle of Tocarema, Juan de Sanct Martín killed the main cacique of the Panche in a fight in which he himself was wounded. Together with the Muisca guecha, the alliance then defeated the Panche. Later, under Hernán Pérez de Quesada's orders, Juan de Céspedes and Juan de Sanct Martín tortured the zipa Sagipa by cutting and burning the soles of his feet, to make him give up his valuables.

literature.text: Felipe Guamán Poma de Ayala, an indigenous Peruvian, finished a handwritten chronicle around 1615 and sent it to King Philip III of Spain. He meant it as a history of the Andes from the earliest human beings to the Incas and the Spanish conquest, and as a call of attention to the problems caused by Spanish government.
literature.source_title: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno
tags: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno

literature.text: Indigenous and mestizo chroniclers wrote in Peru during the colonial period, and many of the indigenous ones, such as Titu Cusi Yupanqui, were of royal Incan bloodlines. Their works record Inca myths, memories of the conquest and life under Spanish rule.

Spanish chroniclers also wrote about the conquest. Francisco Xerez, personal secretary of Pizarro, wrote the Verdadera relación de la conquista del Perú in 1534, and Pedro Sancho de la Hoz's La Conquista de Peru appeared in the same year.

The Huarochirí manuscript, written in Classical Quechua in the late 16th century, is the only surviving written source recording a prehispanic Andean religious tradition in an Andean language. It has been called "the closest thing to an Andean bible".

Almost half of Guamán Poma's book is a description and harsh critique of Spanish colonial rule, which scholars consider uniquely valuable and reliable as a historical source. The book also holds many detailed illustrations that are often reproduced in books and articles about pre-conquest and colonial Peru.
literature.source_title: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno
tags: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno

literature.text: Titu Cusi Yupanqui wrote his Relación de cómo los españoles entraron en Pirú in 1570, after familiarizing himself with Spanish culture. In it he presents his own vision of history, with Incan creation myths, traditions and customs, and impressions of the conquest and colonial dominance.
tags: Relación de cómo los españoles entraron en Pirú

literature.text: Pedro Cieza de León's Crónica del Perú was published in four volumes. Its first volume appeared in 1550, while El señorío de los Incas was composed between 1548 and 1550 but first published in 1873.
The Huarochirí Manuscript is a 17th-century text on indigenous Andean mythology and religion. José María Arguedas later translated it, and it is also known as Hombres y dioses de Huarochirí.

The Huarochirí manuscript was forgotten for centuries in the royal library of Madrid. Hermann Trimborn found it and published a bilingual edition in 1939. In 1966 José María Arguedas translated it into Spanish for the first time.
Guamán Poma dedicated his chronicle to Philip III in the hope of improving colonial rule. There is no evidence that the king ever saw the book.
literature.source_title: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno
tags: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno

literature.text: Guamán Poma's manuscript was never published in its time, and its location for centuries was unknown. Richard Pietschmann rediscovered it at the Royal Danish Library in Copenhagen in 1908, and Paul Rivet published a facsimile edition in Paris in 1936.
literature.source_title: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno
tags: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno

literature.text: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti Yamqui Salcamaygua wrote the Relación de antiguedades deste reyno del Piru in 1613. In it he crudely attempts to explain the Inca cosmogony in rudimentary Spanish.
tags: Relación de antiguedades deste reyno del Piru

literature.text: The cleric Francisco de Ávila, who was responsible for eradicating pagan beliefs, recorded and annotated the Huarochirí manuscript. It is therefore considered ironic that the manuscript now preserves those very beliefs.

Some researchers believe Guamán Poma's manuscript traveled from Spain to Denmark via the library of the Count-Duke of Olivares, part of which was sold to Cornelius Pedersen Lerche, Denmark's ambassador in Spain. This is only speculation.
literature.source_title: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno
tags: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno

literature.text: Cieza de León's fourth volume was divided into five books on the civil wars of the conquest. They were La guerra de las salinas, La guerra de Chupas, La guerra de Quito, La guerra de la Huarina and La guerra de Jaquijaguana.

science.text: Potosí's Cerro Rico was the richest source of silver in the history of mankind. From the 16th to the 18th century, 80% of the world's silver supply came out of this mine, and the Spanish Empire began extracting it in 1545 using forced labor. Harsh conditions in the mines and refining patios killed many miners, and it is believed around eight million died in total. Other sources estimate "hundreds of thousands" and say the eight million was the death toll for the whole Viceroyalty of Peru. The mountain became known as the "mountain that eats men."

By 1565, Cerro Rico at Potosí had run out of high-grade silver ores. Extraction began anew with the patio process, which used mercury to form silver amalgams and extract silver from low-grade ores. Because of the mercury and the huge amount of silver extracted, mercury poisoning was common among the Amerindian laborers, and it caused many miners to die.

Cinchona bark from Peru, known as Jesuit's bark or Peruvian bark, became one of the most valuable commodities shipped from Peru to Europe. It was a successful medicine against malaria, a disease that in the 17th century had caused the deaths of several popes, many cardinals and countless common Roman citizens. It remained the antimalarial drug of choice until the 1940s.

Mercury was necessary to extract silver from the ores of Peru and Potosí using amalgamation processes. It was so essential that mercury consumption was the basis on which the royal fifth, the tax on precious metals, was levied.

The patio process was invented by the Spanish merchant Bartolomé de Medina in 1554. It used mercury amalgamation to extract silver from lower-grade ores, including those containing silver sulfide typical of the unoxidized ores found deeper in the mountain.

In 1609 Alvaro Alonso Barba invented the faster pan process in Potosí. Ore was mixed with salt and mercury, sometimes with copper(II) sulfate, and heated in shallow copper vessels. Treatment time fell from weeks under the patio process to 10 to 20 hours.

The mercury deposits of Huancavelica were disclosed in 1564 or 1566 by the Indian Nahuincopa to his master Jerónimo Luis de Cabrera. The Spanish Crown appropriated them in 1570 and operated them until Peruvian independence in 1821. They eliminated the need to ship mercury from Almadén.

In the 17th century malaria was endemic to the swamps and marshes around Rome, and had caused the deaths of several popes, many cardinals and countless common Roman citizens. The Jesuit apothecary Agostino Salumbrino, who lived in Lima, observed the Quechua using cinchona bark to treat shivering. At the first opportunity he sent a small quantity to Rome for testing as a malaria treatment.
Before the patio process, Potosí miners fed rich oxidized ores directly into small clay "flower pot" furnaces called guayras. These furnaces had been used by the Incas.

In 1648 the Viceroy of Peru judged that Spain could dispense with Potosí's silver if necessary, but not with Huancavelica's mercury. He called the two places the pillars that support the kingdom of Peru and that of Spain.

Whether patio or pan amalgamation was used at a particular location often depended on climate and fuel. Warmer conditions speeded the patio process, while pan amalgamation depended on the availability and cost of fuel to heat the pans.

In 1786 the main mine at Huancavelica suffered a sudden collapse that killed over 100 persons and greatly reduced output. Production rose again through the legalization of scavenging known as pallaqueo, peaking in 1794 to 1796.

politics.text: In 1532, 168 Spanish soldiers under Francisco Pizarro captured the last Sapa Inca, Atahualpa, at the Battle of Cajamarca. The Spaniards fired volleys of gunfire into a vulnerable mass of unarmed Incas and charged with cavalry; the battle is often called a massacre, with 2,000 Incas slain and only one Spanish soldier wounded. It was the first step in a long campaign of decades of fighting that ended in Spanish victory in 1572, and the region was then colonized as the Viceroyalty of Peru.
politics.source_title: Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire

politics.text: In 1542 the Spanish created the Viceroyalty of New Castile, which soon came to be called the Viceroyalty of Peru. It was not properly organized until Francisco de Toledo arrived as viceroy in 1569. Lima, founded in January 1535, was the base from which political and administrative institutions were organized.
politics.source_title: Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire

politics.text: The Bourbon Reforms increased taxes and partitioned the Viceroyalty of Peru as silver production declined in the 18th century. The new laws provoked Túpac Amaru II's rebellion, which lasted from 1780 to 1783. It became the largest revolt in the colonial Americas.

Túpac Amaru II's rebellion began in the Cusco region and extended to modern-day Bolivia and Argentina. It cooperated with other uprisings, such as those led by Tomás and Túpac Katari. The Spanish suppressed all of these revolts.

After the Spanish took Cusco, Manco Inca retreated to the mountains of Vilcabamba and set up the small Neo-Inca State. He and his successors held some power there for several more decades. His son Túpac Amaru, the last Inca, was killed by the Spanish in 1572. Manco had earlier rebelled because Pizarro's brothers Juan and Gonzalo so mistreated him while he was left in Cuzco in 1535.
politics.source_title: Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire

politics.text: From 1532, when Francisco Pizarro invaded the Inca empire, until Toledo arrived in 1569, Spanish rule of the Andean population was largely indirect. Except for Catholic priests, Spaniards were forbidden from living among the Indians, and tribute and labor were extracted through indigenous leaders called caciques or kurakas. Even so, the Andean population was devastated by the internal wars of Spaniards and Incas, the ravages of European diseases, and forced, brutal labor in silver and mercury mines.

Throughout the eighteenth century, the Spanish could not govern the provinces far from Lima without the help of local elites. These elites governed under the title of Curaca and took pride in their Incan history. Indigenous people also rebelled repeatedly during that century.

Toledo ended the Neo-Inca State in Vilcabamba and executed the Inca Túpac Amaru. He resettled the indigenous people in Spanish-style settlements called reductions. He also increased silver production at Potosí by using the mita, an Inca institution of forced labor for mandatory public service. The mines also poisoned people: mercury intoxication played a steady but lethal role in the decline of the native population, and the Spanish also used African slaves alongside captive Incas in mining.
politics.source_title: Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire

politics.text: As parish priest of Huarochirí, Francisco de Ávila built a system of economic exploitation over his indigenous parishioners. He grew rich through forced labor, illegal taxes, and unauthorized commercial monopolies. By 1607 the communities, led by their local native lords (curacas), formally accused him before the Archiatric Court of Lima of severe corruption, extortion, and systemic violence. He was jailed, but the ecclesiastical authorities accepted his argument that the accusations were a conspiracy and acquitted him, and he returned with new inquisitorial powers.

In July 1529 the Queen of Spain signed a charter allowing Pizarro to conquer the Incas. Pizarro was named governor and captain of all conquests in Peru, which the Spanish now called New Castile. He had traveled to Spain after an expedition in 1529 to obtain royal approval.

philosophy.text: Spanish conquerors not only conquered Peru militarily but also sought to convert the indigenous populations to Christianity. Indigenous Andean religious beliefs and practices persisted, and the Catholic Church sought to suppress them. The result was a religious syncretism combining Catholicism with the ancient Inca religion.

Francisco de Ávila, a priest born in Cusco around 1573, became a judge in the campaigns for the extirpation of idolatries. Returning to Huarochirí in 1608, he destroyed thousands of sacred indigenous objects, ordered the public flogging of native priests, and exhumed and burned ancestral mummies.

Early in his assessment of the Andes, Francisco de Toledo idealized a universal resettlement to transform Andeans "from savages to men and from barbarians to civilized people." The plan was part of reforms he had been conceptualizing since 1567 and consulting about with Spanish authorities. It was carried out through the forcible relocation of about 1.4 million native people into approximately 840 reductions, under the violent coercion of Spanish forces, and the people experienced immense hardship.

Around 1608, Francisco de Ávila ordered literate indigenous assistants to record the oral histories, myths, and ancestral traditions of Huarochirí in their native tongue. He wanted to identify and destroy hidden pagan beliefs. The resulting Huarochirí Manuscript is considered the most important source for understanding Inca mythology and Andean religion.

The last public religious ceremony of the Muisca, who lived in the central highlands of the Colombian Andes, was performed in Ubaque on December 27, 1563. Their religion honored Chía, goddess of the Moon, and her husband Sué, god of the Sun, whose pairing showed the complementary character of man and woman.

In 1605, some Dominican nuns built the Convent of Santa Catalina in Cuzco atop the site of the acllahuasi, once home to virginal young women dedicated to serving the ruling Inca. Colonial Catholicism thus literally rose on the foundations of Inca religious institutions.

Researchers such as Peter Gow and Brabec de Mori argue that ayahuasca use developed alongside the Jesuit missions after the 17th century. Ayahuasca chants called ícaros are always sung in Quechua, a lingua franca along the Jesuit and Franciscan missions, no matter the linguistic background of the group.

Ayahuasca cosmology often mirrors Catholicism. The brew is thought to be the body of ayahuascamama, imbibed like the wine and bread taken as the body and blood of Jesus Christ in the Christian Eucharist. Brabec de Mori called this "Christian camouflage" but suggested the practice evolved entirely within these mission contexts.

culture.text: The Muisca worshipped Chía, goddess of the Moon, and her husband Sué, god of the Sun, rather than honouring the supreme being Chiminigagua directly. Presenting the two celestial bodies as husband and wife showed the complementary character of man and woman and the sacred status of marriage.

Religion in Peru is traditionally a syncretism of Catholicism with the ancient Inca religion after the Spanish Conquest. Spanish conquerors sought to convert the indigenous populations, and the Catholic Church tried to suppress Andean beliefs and practices. Those beliefs nonetheless persisted.

Francisco de Ávila returned to Huarochirí in 1608 as a judge-extirpator and launched a massive campaign of religious repression. He systematically destroyed thousands of sacred indigenous objects, ordered the public flogging of native priests, and exhumed and burned ancestral mummies. In 1609, at an auto-da-fé in Lima's main square, he publicly humiliated the native leadership and burned the sacred remains of the local goddess Chaupi Ñamca.

The Muisca held their rituals at sacred sites, both natural ones such as Lake Guatavita, the Siecha Lakes and Lake Tota, and constructed ones. The Sun Temple stood in Suamox, called the "Rome" or "Mecca" of the Muisca, and the Moon Temple in Chía. Priests called obgues performed sacrifices, sometimes human. According to the chroniclers, a family would give one boy to the priests, who raised him as a holy person; at fifteen (other sources say twelve) he was sacrificed, by cutting the heart out of the body or by piercing it with spears. At the Cojines del Zaque these victims were sacrificed to Sué just after sunrise.

In 1607, indigenous communities in Huarochirí, led by their local native lords called curacas, organized a legal and political revolt against Francisco de Ávila. He had used his post as parish priest to enrich himself through forced labor, illegal taxes, and unauthorized commercial monopolies. They accused him before the Archiatric Court of Lima of severe corruption, extortion and systemic violence. He was arrested, stripped of his duties and jailed in Lima pending trial, but was later acquitted.

The last public religious ceremony of the Muisca was performed in Ubaque on December 27, 1563. Its trial has been studied by modern scholars as a final glimpse of Muisca public worship under Spanish rule.

The Convent of Santa Clara was one of the first institutions the conquistadores of Cuzco built for Indian nobles, the daughters of the indigenous elite. There, Inca nobles were to be raised Christian and to receive buenas costumbres, an education in Spanishness that included stitchery and literacy. After the course, students were free to profess vows or leave.

Spanish chronicler Pedro Cieza de León remarked that the Chachapoyas were unusually fair-skinned and famously beautiful among the indigenous Peruvians. He also noted that, after being annexed to the Inca Empire, they adopted customs imposed by the Cusco-based Inca. Their later history was grim: after Spanish soldiers arrived in the city of Chachapoyas by 1547, residents were relocated to Spanish-style towns, and disease, poverty and attrition cut the population, by some accounts by 90% over 200 years.

The Muisca god Chaquén was the god of fertility of the Earth and of sports. He was said to have trained the Muisca for war, and guecha warriors and farmers honoured him to win battles and gain good harvests. He was also the creator of the Colombian national sport, tejo.
